claims.text: mentoring-plan.md lines 3-7: mentoring is an ongoing relationship where an experienced person helps a less experienced one grow through real work, questions and feedback, not by handing over answers; the plan applies to every new developer; all durations are assumptions.

mentoring-plan.md lines 9-15: first week = run the lab with scripts/up.sh per STAGE.md, read STAGE.md and the ADR list in docs/adr/README.md, merge one small change through pull request, CI and review.

mentoring-plan.md lines 19-27: three steps on real sprint work, at least one task each: pair (newcomer at the keyboard most of the time); work alone with a closer review explaining each comment's reason; own a change from story to production incl. canary and release note.
mentoring-plan.md lines 29-30: the newcomer moves up a step when mentor and newcomer both find the current step familiar, not by number of weeks.

mentoring-plan.md lines 34-37: when stuck, the mentor first asks 'Where have you looked?', then points to an ADR, a runbook in docs/runbooks/ or a design document before giving the answer, so the newcomer learns where answers live.

mentoring-plan.md lines 39-41: decisions explained in ADRs and review comments let a mentor help more people than they mentor directly; others read the reasons and take the next decision without asking.

mentoring-plan.md lines 45-47 and on-call-staffing.md lines 49-56: on-call follows three steps: one shadow shift (receives every page with the person on call, watches, does not decide), one shift as primary with a named second, then the rotation.
claims.source_hint: docs/team/mentoring-plan.md @ stage-4 lines 43-47; docs/team/on-call-staffing.md @ stage-4 lines 49-56

claims.text: mentoring-plan.md lines 51-53: mentoring is planned team work, not after-hours work; the mentor takes fewer sprint tasks (project assumption: about one fifth fewer) and the team counts that when choosing sprint work.
mentoring-plan.md lines 55-56: a weekly 30-minute 1-1 between mentor and newcomer; feedback goes both ways, the newcomer says what in the mentoring helps and what does not.

mentoring-plan.md lines 60-68: at the 1-1 the two pick the next task together: one touching a part the newcomer has not changed yet (team-structure.md), one practising their lowest-rated kind of document (architecture-skills-checklist.md); promotion and pay are left out.
review-comments-examples.md lines 7-9: the must-fix example names OrderService.Cancel, cites acceptance criterion 3 and ends with a question.
Each step gives the newcomer more of the work and the mentor less; fixing a problem for someone helps today's task but does not teach where answers live, so similar questions return.
Trade-offs: fixing it for them fits when an incident is running; leaving them alone rarely fits; a career chat is a complement, not the mentoring; graduated real work is the plan's choice.

Choices: in a SEV1 help directly, revisit at the next 1-1 (judgment; lines 34-37 skip incidents); if the mentor's lighter load is dropped, raise it at sprint planning (51-53); newcomer wants to skip step 1: agree on one task showing it is familiar (29-30, 55-56).

Symptoms (hedged): the same person asks the same kind of question for months; a newcomer has talked goals for months but never owned a change through release; decisions in one part wait for one person.
Try it: 1 follows (lines 34-37); 2 breaks (29-30); 3 breaks, shadow shift skipped (45-47); 4 follows (23-25); 5 breaks (51-53).

beyond_scope: Section 5 mentions the first week (lines 9-15) and choosing the next task (lines 60-65) as context; section 7 places incident response ahead of the stuck-question rule (opinion).
